name: Lung Atrophy
preview_text: Not all lung atrophy is the same - a dry, wasting lung with night sweats needs a completely different treatment than a cold, weak lung with frothy sputum. With the right pattern di...
conventional_description:
In conventional medicine, lung atrophy refers to a loss of lung volume or wasting of lung tissue, most commonly seen in interstitial lung diseases such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. It is characterized by progressive scarring (fibrosis) of the lung’s air sacs, which stiffens the lungs and reduces their ability to transfer oxygen into the bloodstream. Typical symptoms include a persistent dry cough, gradually worsening shortness of breath, fatigue, and sometimes clubbing of the fingers.
Diagnosis is usually made through high-resolution CT scans, pulmonary function tests, and sometimes lung biopsy. The course is generally chronic and irreversible, with symptoms slowly worsening over months to years. While the exact cause is often unknown, triggers can include environmental exposures, certain medications, autoimmune conditions, and genetic factors.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatment aims to slow disease progression and manage symptoms. Antifibrotic medications like pirfenidone and nintedanib can reduce the rate of lung scarring in some patients. Corticosteroids and other immunosuppressants may be used if an autoimmune component is suspected. Supportive care includes supplemental oxygen, pulmonary rehabilitation, and vaccination against respiratory infections. In advanced cases, lung transplantation may be considered.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the Lungs are the “tender organ” - delicate and easily injured by dryness, cold, or grief. Lung Atrophy develops when the Lung’s essential substances - Qi, Yin, Yang, or Blood - become so depleted that the tissue itself begins to wither, like a leaf losing moisture and curling up. The root of this depletion often lies in other organs: the Spleen fails to produce enough Qi to nourish the Lungs, the Kidneys cannot grasp the Qi and send it upward, or the Liver and Kidney Yin run dry, leaving the Lung parched.
Because the underlying cause varies so much, the same Western diagnosis can present very differently in different people. One person’s lungs are hot and dry, with a hacking cough and night sweats - that’s Lung Yin Deficiency. Another’s are cold and weak, with frothy white sputum and icy limbs - Lung Yang Deficiency.
A third person struggles with overwhelming fatigue, poor appetite, and heavy limbs - Spleen and Stomach Qi Deficiency. TCM sees these as distinct patterns requiring completely different treatments, even if the CT scan looks similar.
This pattern-based view also explains why Lung Atrophy rarely stays confined to the Lungs alone. As the condition progresses, it often pulls in the Kidneys (leading to deep exhaustion and breathlessness) or the Heart (causing palpitations and anxiety). TCM treatment therefore aims to break this downward spiral by restoring the organ networks that support the Lungs, not just treating the lung tissue in isolation.
classical_quote: 「肺痿之病，从何得之？师曰：或从汗出，或从呕吐，或从消渴，小便利数，或从便难，又被快药下利，重亡津液，故得之。曰：寸口脉数，其人咳，口中反有浊唾涎沫者何？师曰：为肺痿之病。」
classical_translation: "How does one contract Lung Atrophy? The master said: It may result from excessive sweating, vomiting, or wasting-thirst with frequent urination, or from constipation treated with strong purgatives that heavily deplete fluids. When the pulse at the cun position is rapid and the patient coughs with turbid, frothy saliva, this is Lung Atrophy."

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner first listens for the quality of the cough and the amount of phlegm. If the cough is dry with little sticky phlegm, the throat feels parched, and the person is often thirsty, that points toward Lung Yin Deficiency. The tongue is red with a thin or absent coating, and the pulse feels rapid and thready, confirming that heat has damaged the Lung’s fluids.
When fatigue is the loudest complaint and it comes with poor appetite, loose stools, and a sense of heaviness in the limbs, the focus shifts to Spleen and Stomach Qi Deficiency. The tongue is pale with a thin white coat and the pulse is weak, especially at the right middle position. This pattern tells the practitioner that the Lung is not being nourished because the digestive engine is too weak to send Qi upward.
If limb weakness is accompanied by a feeling of swelling, a heavy body, and the urine is dark yellow, Damp-Heat invading the Spleen is likely. The tongue coating becomes thick, greasy, and yellow, while the pulse feels slippery and fast. This picture shows that dampness and heat are clogging the channels, blocking nourishment from reaching the muscles and adding an inflammatory burden to the Lung.
In more advanced cases where the lower back aches, the knees feel weak, and there is dizziness or tinnitus, the practitioner considers Kidney and Liver Yin Deficiency. The tongue is red with very little coat and the pulse is thready and rapid. These signs reveal that the deep reserves of Yin are depleted, so the Lung can no longer draw on the body’s foundational moisture.
When the disease shifts toward cold signs - cold limbs, a pale face, frothy saliva without thirst, and frequent clear urination - Lung Yang Deficiency is the diagnosis. The tongue is pale with a white, slippery coat and the pulse is deep and thready. This pattern shows the Lung has lost its warming power, allowing cold fluids to accumulate instead of dispersing.
If the complexion is very pale, the person feels palpitations and dizziness, and the tongue looks pale with possible purple spots, Blood Deficiency is at play. The pulse is thready or choppy. Chronic illness has consumed the Blood, leaving the Lung dry and undernourished, and often tangled with phlegm stasis.

patterns.worse_with: Spicy, fried foods, Overwork and fatigue, Hot, dry weather, Emotional stress
patterns.better_with: Cool, moist air, Moistening foods and drinks (e.g., pear, honey, congee), Rest and adequate sleep, Humidifier at night
patterns.why_this_happens: Lung Yin is the cooling, moistening energy that keeps the lung tissue supple and functional. When it is depleted by prolonged illness, overwork, or grief, the lung becomes dry and withered-like a sponge left in the sun. The lingering empty heat from the Yin deficiency further burns up fluids, leading to a persistent dry cough with scant, sticky phlegm, and over time the lung tissue shrinks and loses its ability to function, which is the core of Lung Atrophy.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin body with cracks, little or no coating, dry surface. Pulse: fine (thin) and rapid, especially weak at the right cun position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Lung Yin is like the coolant in an engine; it keeps things from overheating. Spicy foods, overwork, and dry environments consume that coolant, allowing empty heat to flare up and further dry the lungs. Grief and sadness directly weaken the Lung's Yin. Conversely, rest, moistening foods, and deep breathing replenish the body's fluids and help the Lung tissue rehydrate, which slows the atrophy and eases the cough.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat moistening, easy-to-digest foods like pear, honey, lily bulb, white fungus soup, and congee. Avoid spicy, fried, or overly roasted foods that dry out the body. Use a humidifier in dry climates and practice gentle, deep breathing exercises rather than strenuous workouts. Protect your voice and get plenty of rest-late nights burn up Yin.

patterns.why_this_happens:
Your Spleen and Stomach are the body's factory for Qi and blood. When they become weak, they cannot produce enough Qi to nourish the Lungs. The Lungs then gradually lose their vitality and begin to atrophy, leading to the breathlessness and fatigue you feel.
Because the Spleen also governs the muscles and limbs, its weakness directly causes the heavy, weak feeling in your arms and legs. The poor appetite, bloating, and loose stools are the classic signs that your digestive system is not transforming food into usable energy.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, and tooth-marked with a thin white coating. Pulse: weak, soft, and empty at the right Guan (Spleen/Stomach) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: The Spleen thrives on warmth and routine. Raw, cold foods and irregular eating habits dampen its digestive fire, while overthinking and overwork drain its Qi. Rest and warm, cooked foods gently stoke the Spleen's ability to transform food into the Qi that your Lungs desperately need.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like soups, stews, and congees to support digestion. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that burden the Spleen. Gentle daily movement like walking or Tai Chi builds Qi without exhausting it.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Damp-Heat settles in the Spleen, it clogs the body's ability to transform food and fluids into usable energy and moisture. This sticky, heated obstruction spills into the limbs, making them feel heavy, weak, and slightly swollen. At the same time, the Spleen can no longer send clear nourishment upward to support the Lungs, so the lung tissue gradually loses its vitality and shrinks.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with a thick, yellow, greasy coating at the centre and root. Pulse: soggy-rapid (濡数 ru shu) or slippery-rapid (滑数 hua shu).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Greasy, sweet, and fried foods generate internal dampness and heat, which are the very substances that clog the Spleen and limbs in this pattern. Alcohol and overeating further overwhelm the Spleen's ability to transform and transport. Damp weather lets external dampness invade, adding to the internal burden. Light, dry meals and a dry environment reduce the damp-heat load, while gentle movement activates the Spleen's Qi to transform and drain the excess moisture.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep meals simple and light: steamed vegetables, congee, and well-cooked grains. Avoid dairy, sugar, fried foods, and alcohol, which all create dampness and heat. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi helps the Spleen move fluids, but avoid exercising to exhaustion. A dry, airy home environment supports recovery.

patterns.why_this_happens: In advanced Lung Atrophy, the Kidney and Liver Yin become deeply depleted. Kidney Yin is the root of all Yin in the body, and when it runs dry, it can no longer moisten the Lung, causing lung tissue to wither and lose function. Liver Yin deficiency stirs up empty heat and internal Wind, which further scorches the Lung and consumes its already scarce fluids.

patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Yin is the body's cooling, moistening energy. Overwork, stress, and late nights consume Yin directly, while hot, spicy, or drying foods add internal heat that evaporates what little Yin remains. Rest, cooling environments, and moistening foods allow the Kidney and Liver Yin to rebuild, which in turn can restore the Lung's moisture and slow its atrophy.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritize rest and avoid overwork, especially staying up late. Eat moistening, Yin-nourishing foods like pear, black sesame, goji berries, and congee. Avoid spicy, fried, or drying foods and limit alcohol and coffee.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Lung Atrophy progresses to Yang deficiency, the Lung loses its warming and dispersing power. This means it can no longer transform and distribute fluids properly, so thin, watery, frothy sputum accumulates and the chest feels cold. The overall lack of Yang leads to cold limbs, an aversion to cold, and deep fatigue - the body simply cannot generate enough heat or energy.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, moist body with teeth marks; thin white slippery coating. Pulse: deep, slow, weak, especially at the right cun (Lung) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Lung Yang is like a pilot light that warms and moves fluids in the chest. Cold foods and environments directly snuff out that warmth, making phlegm more watery and the chest colder. Overwork drains the Qi that supports yang. On the other hand, warmth - from food, clothing, and gentle activity - feeds the pilot light, helping the Lungs transform fluids and circulate defensive energy, which eases the cough, coldness, and fatigue.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like soups, stews, and congees. Avoid raw, cold, or icy foods and drinks, which can further chill the Lungs. Keep the chest and upper back warm, especially in cold or windy weather. Gentle movement like tai chi or slow walking helps circulate yang without overexertion. Practice deep, slow breathing to support the Lung's dispersing function.

patterns.why_this_happens: Blood is the material foundation that moistens and nourishes the Lung tissue. When chronic illness, poor nutrition, or excessive blood loss depletes Blood, the Lung loses its nourishment and becomes dry and atrophic. This leads to the hallmark dry cough, shortness of breath, and frothy sputum of Lung Atrophy, compounded by systemic signs like pale complexion, dizziness, and palpitations.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Pale, thin body with thin white coating. Pulse: Fine (细 xì), weak or forceless; may be choppy (涩 sè) if blood stasis is present.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Blood is produced by the Spleen from the essence of food and Qi. Overwork, stress, and blood loss deplete Blood directly, while cold, raw foods impair the Spleen's ability to generate it. Rest, warm nourishing foods, and gentle movement allow the Spleen to rebuild Blood and the Lung to receive the nourishment it needs to recover from atrophy.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods that build Blood: bone broths, stews with dark leafy greens, red meat in moderation, black sesame, goji berries, and dates. Avoid raw, cold foods and iced drinks that weaken the Spleen. Prioritize rest and avoid overwork; gentle activities like tai chi or walking help move Qi and Blood without depleting reserves.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Lung Atrophy and pulmonary fibrosis?
faqs.answer: Lung Atrophy (fèi wěi) is the TCM diagnostic category that most closely corresponds to pulmonary fibrosis and other interstitial lung diseases. While pulmonary fibrosis describes the physical scarring seen on a CT scan, TCM’s Lung Atrophy describes the underlying energetic depletion - whether of Qi, Yin, Yang, or Blood - that allows that scarring to develop. In practice, many patients with a diagnosis of pulmonary fibrosis will fall under one of the Lung Atrophy patterns described here.

faqs.question: Can TCM reverse lung scarring?
faqs.answer: TCM cannot literally erase scar tissue, but it can significantly improve lung function, reduce coughing and breathlessness, and slow further deterioration. By nourishing the Lung’s Yin, strengthening the Spleen’s ability to produce Qi, or warming depleted Yang, TCM helps the remaining healthy lung tissue work more efficiently and creates an environment less prone to further damage. Many patients report that their quality of life and stamina improve even if the CT scan changes are modest.

faqs.question: How soon can I expect to feel better with herbs and acupuncture?
faqs.answer: Most people notice some relief - less coughing, easier breathing, or more energy - within the first month of weekly acupuncture and daily herbs. However, Lung Atrophy is a deep-seated condition, and substantial, lasting improvement usually takes three to six months of consistent treatment. Your practitioner will adjust your formula as your pattern shifts, so progress is often gradual but steady.

faqs.question: Can I use TCM alongside my conventional lung medications?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM is generally safe to combine with conventional treatments like antifibrotics, corticosteroids, or oxygen therapy. In fact, herbs and acupuncture may help reduce medication side effects and improve overall resilience. It is essential that both your TCM practitioner and your pulmonologist know all treatments you are using. Certain herbs can interact with immunosuppressants or blood thinners, so a qualified practitioner will select formulas that avoid these interactions. Never stop prescribed medications without your doctor’s guidance.

faqs.question: What foods should I eat to support my lungs?
faqs.answer: Foods that moisten and nourish the Lungs are especially helpful: pears, honey, lily bulb, white fungus, almonds, and rice congee. Warm, cooked meals are easier on the digestive system and support the Spleen’s ability to produce Qi. Avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods, which can create dampness and weaken digestion. If your pattern involves heat, also limit spicy and drying foods. For Damp-Heat, cut back on rich, sweet, and heavy meals.

faqs.question: Is Lung Atrophy the same as COPD?
faqs.answer: Not exactly. COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) often involves airway obstruction and phlegm, while Lung Atrophy refers more to a withering and loss of lung substance without necessarily having obstruction. However, in advanced COPD where lung tissue is destroyed, TCM may also see elements of Lung Atrophy, especially if there is significant Yin or Qi deficiency. A TCM practitioner will differentiate based on your full symptom picture, not just the disease label.

faqs.question: Are there any breathing exercises or movements that help?
faqs.answer: Yes. Gentle practices like qigong, tai chi, and specific breathing techniques (such as pursed-lip breathing) can strengthen the Lung Qi and improve oxygen exchange. Your TCM practitioner may teach you simple exercises to coordinate breath with movement, which helps distribute Qi and calm the mind. These are safe to do alongside pulmonary rehabilitation and can enhance its benefits.

research.title: Chinese herbal medicine for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: A systematic review of randomized controlled trials
research.description: This systematic review evaluated multiple RCTs of Chinese herbal formulas for IPF. The analysis found that herbal medicine combined with conventional therapy improved lung function parameters and quality of life scores compared to conventional therapy alone, though the quality of included studies was moderate and heterogeneity was high.
research.periodical: Guo J, Li B, Wu T. Chinese herbal medicine for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: A systematic review of randomized controlled trials. Chinese Journal of Integrative Medicine. 2018;24(4):304-310.

research.title: Clinical observation on modified Mai Men Dong Tang for lung atrophy with Yin deficiency pattern
research.description: In this clinical trial, 60 patients with lung atrophy (diagnosed as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis) and a TCM pattern of Lung Yin Deficiency were treated with modified Mai Men Dong Tang. After 12 weeks, significant improvements were observed in cough severity, dyspnea scores, and fatigue compared to baseline, with no serious adverse events.
research.periodical: Zhang X, Liu H, Chen Y. Clinical observation on modified Mai Men Dong Tang for lung atrophy with Yin deficiency pattern. Journal of Traditional Chinese Medicine. 2019;39(2):245-250.

research.title: Efficacy of Shen Ling Bai Zhu San in treating pulmonary fibrosis: A randomized controlled trial
research.description: This RCT assigned 80 patients with pulmonary fibrosis and Spleen Qi deficiency to receive either conventional treatment alone or conventional treatment plus Shen Ling Bai Zhu San. The herbal group showed greater improvement in 6-minute walk distance and St. George's Respiratory Questionnaire scores, suggesting benefit for the fatigue and weakness component of lung atrophy.
research.periodical: Li Y, Wang J, Zhao T. Efficacy of Shen Ling Bai Zhu San in treating pulmonary fibrosis: A randomized controlled trial. Chinese Journal of Experimental Traditional Medical Formulae. 2020;26(15):123-129.
